readingInstruction: Read 2 Kings 3:1-4:44. Elisha’s ministry begins with the defeat of Moab and a series of miracles of provision and restoration. Look for how these miracles echo the work of Elijah and anticipate the work of Jesus.
settingTheScene: Elisha begins his ministry under King Jehoram of Israel, son of Ahab. A coalition of Israel, Judah, and Edom marches against Moab and nearly dies of thirst. Elisha is called, and God provides. Chapter 4 follows with four miracles in the lives of ordinary people: a widow’s oil, a Shunammite woman’s son, a poisoned stew, and a feeding of one hundred men.
observation: The three kings are without water, and Jehoshaphat asks, “Is there no prophet of the LORD here, through whom we may inquire of the LORD?” (3:11).
Elisha says, “You shall not see wind or rain, but that streambed shall be filled with water” (3:17).
The Moabite king sacrifices his son on the wall, and “there came great wrath against Israel” (3:27).
A widow cries, “Your servant my husband is dead… and the creditor has come to take my two children,” and Elisha multiplies her oil (4:1-7).
A woman of Shunem builds a room for Elisha, and God gives her a son (4:8-17).
The boy dies, and the woman says, “It is well,” and Elisha raises him (4:18-37).
Elisha purifies a poisoned stew: “Then bring flour… and there was no harm in the pot” (4:38-41).
He feeds a hundred men with twenty loaves, “For thus says the LORD, They shall eat and have some left” (4:42-44).
interpretation:
Chapter 3 shows God’s mercy to a flawed alliance. Jehoram is no friend of the LORD, but because of Jehoshaphat, Elisha speaks. The water arrives not by rain but by a miracle, and in the morning the sun on the water looks like blood to the Moabites. The victory is God’s gift. The ending is strange and grim: the king of Moab sacrifices his own son, and Israel withdraws. The chapter shows how dark pagan religion could be.

Chapter 4 turns to the ordinary lives of the poor. The widow is about to lose her sons to a creditor. She has only a jar of oil. Elisha tells her to borrow empty vessels, as many as she can, and the oil flows until all the jars are full. God’s provision is limited only by her faith and the number of jars. It is a picture of grace that meets need and overflows.

The Shunammite woman is a model of hospitality. She sees that Elisha is a holy man and builds a small room for him. When she receives a promise of a son, she is incredulous. And when the boy dies, she says, “It is well.” Her faith is mixed with grief, but she goes straight to the man of God. Elisha stretches himself over the boy and he lives. It is the first account of resurrection in the Old Testament after Elijah’s raising of the widow’s son.

The last two miracles are simple. Death in the pot is turned to food, and a small gift of bread feeds a hundred men with some left over. The theme is the same: in a land of famine and idolatry, God’s word brings life and provision. The “sons of the prophets” are fed because of the faithfulness of a few.

Elisha’s miracles are works of mercy. They are directed at the vulnerable. They show what kind of God the LORD is: one who sees the needs of the poor.
connection: Jesus did every one of these miracles on a larger scale. He fed the five thousand with five loaves and two fish, “and they all ate and were satisfied” (Luke 9:12-17). He raised a widow’s son (Luke 7:11-17), and Jairus’s daughter (Luke 8:49-56). He turned water into wine (John 2). He said, “I am the bread of life” (John 6:35). Elisha’s miracles point to the One who has power over death and hunger.
application:
Ask God to show you your “empty jars,” places where you need his provision. Bring them in faith.

Practice hospitality, as the Shunammite did. Whom can you welcome?

When you face a loss, say with the Shunammite, “It is well,” as an act of trust, even through grief.
prayerPrompts: Tell God what vessels in your life feel empty.
Ask him to teach you hospitality.
Thank him that you can say “It is well” in sorrow.
